catalog_quote: 4 Tone. The tone analysis of Mundari is based on the tone of approximately 200 nouns and 100 verbs, and is still tentative. As in its related languages, Mundari is analyzed to have two underlying level tones, High and Low (27). Contour tone consists of more than one level tone on the same syllable. The syllable is the tone-bearing unit, and at most two tones are allowed on the same syllable. Falling tone is only attested on the final syllable of words. The only words attested with a syllable having rising tone are /ŋə̌ᵘŋ/ ‘hyena’ and /rᵘə̌.kə̀/ ‘darkness’. The lexical and grammatical function of tone is low in that there are few tone minimal pairs and few if any grammatical distinctions made solely by tone. (27) H pɛ́ ‘be tired’ wɔ́k ‘arrive’ / L pɛ̀ ‘show, reveal, shoot (gun)’ wɔ̀k ‘beat’

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mundari is described as a tone language with two underlying level tones (H, L), syllable as tone-bearing unit, contour (falling) tone restricted to word-final syllables, and low functional load of tone. The description says nothing at all about word stress or accent; no stress rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (Tone: rising tone attested only in two words; floating L surfaces phrase-finally.)
new_statements.domain_note: Tone data are citation forms and frame-elicited nouns/verbs; no word- or phrase-level stress/prominence is discussed anywhere in the 2014 paper, its 2013 draft, the 2013 SIL grammar book, primer, or dictionary.
new_statements.identity_note: All SIL materials (Stirtz 2014; Lutwori et al. 2013; dictionary) describe Mundari as spoken in Terekeka county north of Juba (speakers from Tarakeka at Juba workshops) = Glottolog mand1425 Mandari [mqu]; Stirtz gives alternate names Mandari, Chir, Kir. Not to be confused with Austroasiatic Mundari (unr) of India, which dominates archive.org search results. Vossen 1982 treats 'Mondari' as the north-westernmost Bari dialect with slight local variants (his informant from Tali Post).

Sec. 4 'Tone' (p. 13) and sec. 5 'Tone morphophonology' describe a two-level (H/L) tone system with the syllable as TBU, falling tone only word-final, polar/floating tones; the words stress, accent, prominence, intonation do not occur anywhere in the paper (a full-text search for stress/accent the text layer).
Lists alphabet and four tone marks (high, low, mid, falling) citing the SIL dictionary; nothing on stress. Used only to locate the webonary file URLs.
